The app works like this: choose VPN, Tor, or VPN + Tor, then choose a whole-device or proxy scenario and configure routing rules for apps and web addresses.
Add a VPN profile from Profiles by importing a v2raytun link, configuration file, or QR code.
Hold the VPN profile area on Home to refresh the current connection’s IP and virtual location; tap it to open saved profiles. A compatible server-backed configuration refreshes before every connection, while holding START refreshes it manually without connecting. Tor can start without a VPN profile.
Hold anywhere in the terminal area to open terminal-history cleanup.
Tap STATUS for the current state and rule sets; hold STATUS for extended status, encryption state, and recent journal entries.
A whole-device scenario tunnels all device traffic; a proxy scenario routes selected apps, and app/web rules act inside that scenario.
Firewall, Tor, I2P and DNS filters are modules that can run beside any mode or without one.
“Atomic scenario application” applies VPN and Tor scenarios without asking; when it is off, every scenario switch asks for confirmation. Network rules always apply atomically.
Supported VPN protocols are VLESS, VMess, Hysteria2, WireGuard, AmneziaWG, Trojan, Shadowsocks, Naive, TUIC, AnyTLS and ShadowTLS.
FoxHole DB downloads only the data sets required by the features you enable.
Settings and profiles are stored locally in encrypted form with keys protected by Android Keystore; you can also require a FoxHole Guard PIN or biometrics in Security.
New-app detection records installs and removals, and quarantine blocks a new app’s network access until you allow it whenever a supported tunnel or the standalone firewall is active.

the “whole device” scenario sends all device traffic into the VPN tunnel; per-app routing rules are ignored in it. the proxy scenario splits into “only the selected apps” and “everything except the selected apps”; per-app routing rules work in it. the scenario is configured in “routing” → app rules; VPN and Tor scenarios are configured separately, but some combinations have compatibility limits: “VPN for the whole device + Tor for selected apps” is allowed, the reverse is not. the local network proxy server is configured in the extras section.

FoxHole Guard does not currently support Tor inside a VPN tunnel for profiles that use a UDP transport: choose a profile with a TCP transport or run Tor beside the VPN. the Tor network carries TCP streams but not arbitrary UDP, so calls and other features that require UDP do not work through Tor; HTTP/HTTPS streaming can work, but may be slow. with Tor inside the VPN, the internet provider sees the VPN connection instead of a direct Tor connection, while the VPN provider may see the connection to a Tor entry relay or bridge and its metadata. the MODE button on the home screen switches between VPN / VPN and Tor / Tor. if the network blocks a direct Tor connection, turn bridges on in the Tor settings: the bridge list comes from FoxHole DB - from the FoxHole DB mirror or straight from the Tor Project.

a smart VPN profile gathers several VPN protocols of one server into a single list for quick switching and testing.
the protocol table shows T/P/L - connect time, server ping and latency - and the S column with each protocol's state: [x] active, [ ] off, [~] testing, [!] unavailable, [?] never measured.
the “test” button runs a test of every available protocol, and ★ marks the best candidates to connect through.
a tap on the S column works as the switch for that protocol.
routing and the rules for apps and web sites

app and web site routing rules apply atomically.
the “whole device” scenario ignores the per-app rules: the rules stay saved and act again in the proxy scenario, which enables per-app routing separately for VPN and Tor - the selected apps' traffic can be sent into the tunnel or excluded from it.
app blocking is in force while a VPN or Tor tunnel is active or the firewall is on.
the firewall raised by I2P in transparent mode applies no rules: no blocking, no DNS interception - only .i2p traffic is diverted.

the main app journal records FoxHole Guard\'s own events and network connections, so that module and extra starts and stops, state changes and the events around them can be read in one place. the network journal shows individual connections with their time, app, protocol, country and the volume of traffic carried. the security journal keeps the events around app changes, FoxHole Sentinel\'s work and detected network traffic anomalies. journals are stored on the device encrypted and are never sent anywhere.

the statistics section collects local statistics of traffic, sessions and DNS events and lets you look at overall totals, VPN profiles, apps, DNS blocks, firewall events, Tor and I2P for the chosen period. collection is off by default and is switched on with the button in the top right corner of the section, where the refresh interval, the retention period and the specific metrics the app should collect are configured separately. statistics are available for a day, a week and a month, are kept locally and never leave the device.

the local firewall blocks internet access for the apps you select and applies those rules while a supported tunnel is active or while the firewall runs on its own. when quarantine is enabled, installing a new app while the firewall or any of the three main operating modes is active blocks that app’s internet access until you decide. manage pending decisions under settings → firewall → module settings.
the FoxHole Guard tile in the quick settings shade lets you start and stop the connection without opening the app, and on start it uses the last connection mode picked on the home screen.

kill switch uses the Android system feature “block connections without VPN”, which - with no active VPN tunnel - blocks the device\'s network traffic at the system level and does not let apps quietly reach the network directly after a connection drops. the feature is enabled in the system VPN settings for FoxHole Guard and is controlled by Android itself.

settings → application → app data: here you can save FoxHole Guard profiles and transferable settings in a portable password-encrypted backup. profiles can contain VPN or subscription credentials, so keep the file and its password separately; a forgotten password cannot be recovered. restore imports the backed-up profiles and applies transferable preferences, but keeps this device\'s app lock, private-update token, Android Usage Access consent, generated local-proxy credentials and local security baselines. the app shows a preview and asks for confirmation first. the same section holds separate clear actions for journals, statistics and profiles, while the full reset deletes all app data and cannot be undone.

DNS settings apply inside a supported tunnel; when device DNS protection is enabled, FoxHole Guard starts a separate local DNS guard, so the selected DNS filtering can also work without VPN or Tor. DNS filtering lists are downloaded from the FoxHole DB DNS data set and enabled in DNS settings, while exclusions keep selected apps or web addresses on the device’s system DNS server.

DNS filtering is not applied to WireGuard or AmneziaWG: WireGuard uses the profile’s DNS server without filtering, and AmneziaWG is not yet supported.

the app also watches the system set of DNS servers, and if the network suddenly replaces the whole set it was using, it writes a warning into the security journal - such a change can be a sign of DNS being altered on the path.

a VPN profile can be bound to a specific Wi-Fi or mobile network, so FoxHole Guard remembers which profile you usually use there. on entering a bound network the app recommends the matching profile with a banner inside FoxHole Guard, or - if the app is closed - with a system notification that switches the profile in one tap.

the proxy server lets you share the route you have raised with other devices on the current local Wi-Fi network over SOCKS5 or HTTP, and send their traffic through the chosen VPN or Tor route.\nauthentication for the local proxy is mandatory, so with an empty password the server does not start.\nthe client ↔ phone hop gets no additional encryption from FoxHole Guard, so use such a proxy only on a trusted local network.

long-press a profile → edit opens the controls for that VPN protocol.
the button in the top-right corner of the VPN Profiles section creates a new VPN protocol from an empty template for any supported protocol.
in a smart profile each protocol is stored as its own entry and edited independently.
using insecure TLS always requires your explicit consent, which is remembered for that profile only.

profiles can be imported from a clipboard link, a configuration file, or a QR code. after a v2raytun subscription is added, FoxHole Guard refreshes it before every connection; hold START with that subscription selected to refresh it manually without connecting. selection mode lets you mark several profiles and export them to a file. with one VPN profile or protocol selected, “share” can copy a link or display its QR code.

settings → security let you protect entry to FoxHole Guard with your own PIN or system biometrics. settings and profiles are already stored locally in encrypted form with keys protected by Android Keystore. system biometrics act as an entry gate and do not re-encrypt that data. with a custom PIN, biometric entry uses a separate auth-per-use Android Keystore key to open the same PIN-protected keybox. the security journal is always sealed separately and hash-chained: biometrics add no separate encryption layer, while after entry FoxHole Guard decrypts the journal and verifies its chain against the anchored checkpoint. sensitive data is never sent to FoxHole Guard servers.

FoxHole Sentinel analyses local system and network metadata rather than the contents of your traffic, and it is not an antivirus, so its signals are meant to surface suspicious changes and behaviour but do not by themselves prove the presence of malicious code. the app check evaluates the install source and the potentially dangerous capabilities an app declares, using local security lists. the security lists, including stalkerware indicators and network IOCs, are built into the release and can be updated through FoxHole DB; the built-in list is built from AssoEchap/stalkerware-indicators (CC-BY-4.0) and covers known stalkerware indicators specifically, not malware in general. the traffic detector compares one-minute total activity windows, and the signals that need to be tied to individual apps or to background activity additionally use local statistics and access to usage history. with the FoxHole Guard password and FoxHole Sentinel event monitoring on, FoxHole Sentinel records app installs, updates and removals, the background host\'s heartbeat and suspicious monitoring gaps into a sealed hash-chained journal. economy mode keeps no permanent service of its own, while reinforced mode runs a persistent service with a visible system notification and can therefore use more power. force-stopping FoxHole Guard through Android pauses monitoring until the app is started again, and FoxHole Sentinel cannot prevent the actions of a user or another process with root access, nor the clearing of the app\'s data.

FoxHole DB is the app\'s data repository, split into four data sets: DNS filtering lists, the Tor bridge list, FoxHole Sentinel security lists, and the geo database with countries and IP ranges. the app downloads only data sets selected by the user or required by explicitly enabled features; every received artifact is verified before use and replaced atomically. settings → updates show the overall FoxHole DB status - “up to date” or “update required” - and let you update data sets manually or enable automatic updates. the geo database is not built into the app: it is selected by default in the setup wizard, but its download can be skipped and run later.

2. FoxHole Guard is not an antivirus. It warns about events and suspicious activity, but does not guarantee detection or blocking of malware.

3. The developers are not liable for consequences resulting from use of the app.

4. By using the app, you also accept the licenses of its components and DNS data sets.

5. By continuing, you confirm that you have read and accept these terms in full.
